tasks.short: Demonstrate products and explain how they meet customer needs.

steps.what: Review product facts, approved claims and demonstration instructions.
Ask about the customer's intended use and relevant constraints.
Demonstrate relevant features, invite participation and explain practical benefits.
Look up unfamiliar questions in approved product documents.

loop.input: A typed product question and retrieved passages from current approved product documents.
loop.output: A short answer draft with source passages, or an unresolved-question flag.
loop.check: Require valid document references and matching product versions; the promoter checks support before speaking.
loop.stop: One retrieval and one draft per question, with a ten-second timeout; missing support falls back to manual lookup or a product specialist.
loop.why_not_simpler: Indexed search handles common questions; varied wording and answers spread across documents can require bounded reading.

steps.what: Answer questions, check understanding and refer unresolved issues to a product specialist.

tasks.design: Configure a product-specific demonstration brief in {DOCS} from approved facts and instructions. Add indexed search and a bounded reading loop through {WORKFLOW} for unfamiliar questions, showing source passages for promoter approval before use.
tasks.previous_blocker: Product documents can be difficult to search during a live interaction. Earlier keyword search struggled with varied wording, while unsourced answers were unsuitable for customer claims.
tasks.enabler_now: Document indexing and bounded reading can produce source-linked drafts. Templates handle the standard brief; the model is reserved for questions that need free-text reading.
tasks.still_hard: Documents may omit limitations or contradict one another. Safe demonstrations, customer understanding and unsupported claims still require human judgement.
tasks.human_edge: Read reactions, adapt the demonstration and distinguish curiosity from a real purchase need.

ambition.what: Visitors who prefer an approved plain-language product explanation.

tasks.altitude: The promoter spends slightly less time searching and can explain a wider range of documented details. They gain discretion to choose approved explanation formats, while technical claims still follow approved sources.

reach.task: Triage technical suitability questions before a specialist demonstration.
reach.learn: Recognise compatibility limits, safety constraints and the evidence needed for escalation.

evidence.claim: Indexed approved documents and bounded reading can support source-linked answer drafts; this digest provides no demonstrator-specific case.
The EU AI Act includes AI literacy duties relevant to staff using the answer tool.

assumptions: Approved product documents are available digitally and have identifiable versions.
Questions are typed without customer identifiers; conversations are not recorded.
The promoter remains the customer-facing speaker.
The answer desk supports existing approved claims rather than creating new claims.
The access range assumes no employee monitoring; any required consultation under national rules needs separate scheduling.
unknowns: Whether indexed search alone answers enough questions to make the model loop unnecessary.
Whether product documents contain reliable limitations and safety guidance.
Which visitors need plain-language materials and whether approved versions already exist.
Whether local access, GDPR or national consultation requirements extend rollout.
research_questions: Does source-linked assistance reduce lookup time during live demonstrations?
How reliably does the loop refuse questions unsupported by current documents?
Do plain-language explanations improve visitor understanding in observed sessions?
new_work: Maintain document versions and remove superseded claims.
Review unanswered questions with a product specialist.
Check a sample of answer drafts for source support.
Train promoters to verify drafts and recognise when to escalate.
tasks.statement: Demonstrate or explain products, methods, or services to persuade customers to purchase products or use services.

tasks.short: Offer samples, coupons and approved information to interested customers.

steps.what: Read the approved offer, eligibility rules and product information.
Prepare suitable samples, coupons and brochures for the session.
Offer suitable incentives, explain conditions and hand materials to customers.
Count unused materials after the session.
Enter counts and calculate material usage in the campaign tally.

tasks.design: Configure a session brief in {DOCS} from approved campaign fields and materials. A short {WORKFLOW} form records opening and closing counts, calculates usage and sends the tally to the campaign coordinator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Most work is physical distribution and customer contact. Small administrative savings rarely justified a separate application.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing templates, forms and arithmetic can remove repeated preparation and tally calculations. AI-assisted coding can reduce setup effort; no model is needed in operation.
tasks.still_hard: Approaching people tactfully, handling samples safely and judging whether an offer suits the customer remain physical and interpersonal work.
tasks.human_edge: Notice hesitation, respect refusals and explain conditions without pressure.
tasks.altitude: The promoter spends slightly less time assembling briefs and completing tallies. Customer contact and decision rights remain unchanged.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of retail sales workers
reach.task: Plan sample replenishment between sessions.
reach.learn: Read usage counts alongside expected footfall, waste and stock limits.

evidence.claim: Templates and count-entry forms can calculate material usage without a model.
Physical sample distribution and customer persuasion remain predominantly human work.

assumptions: A typical campaign supplies approved materials and offer rules.
The design uses aggregate stock counts rather than customer identities.
Time shares are estimates; physical work dominates, consistent with the supplied priors.
The access range covers a simple configuration without employee monitoring.
unknowns: Whether materials are currently tallied in the {SPREADSHEET}, on paper or elsewhere.
Whether samples require food, hygiene, age or other eligibility checks.
Whether employee consultation is required under national rules or existing agreements.
research_questions: Does a count-entry form save time during a real session?
Can opening and closing counts distinguish distribution from waste accurately enough?
new_work: Maintain approved offer versions and effective dates.
Resolve missing counts and record waste separately.
Maintain form access and campaign identifiers.
tasks.statement: Provide product samples, coupons, informational brochures, or other incentives to persuade people to buy products.

tasks.short: Keep the demonstration area tidy and return equipment and materials after use.

steps.what: Clear waste, clean surfaces and keep customer access unobstructed.
Return equipment and unused materials to their designated locations.

tasks.design: Use labelled storage locations and a simple physical reset card, with its master in {DOCS}. No software build is justified for the cleaning and return work.
tasks.previous_blocker: The task requires moving, inspecting and cleaning physical objects. Software cannot perform those actions.
tasks.enabler_now: No technical breakthrough is needed. Clear storage labels and an existing reset procedure are sufficient.
tasks.still_hard: Spills, damaged equipment and unfamiliar venues require local judgement and physical action.
tasks.human_edge: Notice hazards and judge whether equipment and surfaces are ready for the next customer.
tasks.altitude: The promoter's week and decision rights do not materially change. Cleaning and equipment return remain part of each session.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of retail sales workers
reach.task: Arrange shared demonstration storage.
reach.learn: Place frequently used items within easy reach and separate clean, used and damaged equipment.

evidence.claim: Cleaning and returning demonstration equipment require physical work; a digital workflow offers little direct substitution.

assumptions: The demonstration area is small enough for the promoter to reset.
Physical work accounts for essentially all task time.
The supplied communication-heavy activity split is a weak fit for this task; the steps support physical work instead.
unknowns: Which cleaning, hygiene and equipment-isolation procedures apply.
Whether the venue provides suitable storage and waste facilities.
Who handles hazardous spills or damaged equipment.
research_questions: Would changing kit layout remove unnecessary carrying or searching?
new_work: Replace damaged labels and update storage locations when the kit changes.
tasks.statement: Keep areas neat while working and return items to correct locations following demonstrations.

tasks.short: Count demonstration activity, reconcile coupons, and report results.

steps.what: Tally audience questions and participation during the demonstration.
Count remaining coupons and calculate how many were distributed.
Enter tallies into the shared demonstration reporting workbook.
Check totals and correct missing or inconsistent entries.
Send the checked report to the campaign supervisor.

tasks.design: Configure a mobile counter and closing-stock form in the {WORKFLOW}; direct capture removes re-entry into the {SPREADSHEET}. Validation rules produce a report, route inconsistencies to the demonstrator, and notify the campaign supervisor through the {EMAIL} after approval.
tasks.previous_blocker: Activity happens away from a desk. Paper tallies and reporting templates are disconnected.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing forms, counters, validation and notifications can handle this. AI-assisted coding can reduce the effort of adding offline capture or an export.
tasks.still_hard: Someone must notice questions and count physical coupons. Poor connectivity and ambiguous counting definitions remain.
tasks.human_edge: The demonstrator distinguishes a genuine customer question from repeated chatter and explains unusual results.
tasks.altitude: Less of the week goes into copying totals and chasing reports. With delegated stock limits, the demonstrator can request replenishment during a shift.

reach.task: Allocate promotional stock between demonstration locations.
reach.learn: Stock coverage, campaign targets, and the limits of activity counts as evidence of sales.

evidence.claim: Structured counters and stock arithmetic can produce activity reports without a model.
Direct capture removes transcription, but physical observation still needs a person.

assumptions: Step shares and remaining time are planning estimates, not measured results.
The baseline uses paper tallies and a shared reporting workbook.
Coupon distribution means opening stock less closing stock, adjusted for recorded returns or losses.
Reports contain aggregate activity rather than customer identities.
Replenishment authority requires delegation from the campaign supervisor.
Access estimates include checking national rules for employee consultation if individual activity becomes monitoring.
unknowns: Actual counting definitions and reporting template.
Available mobile devices, connectivity, and offline requirements.
Whether the existing {WORKFLOW} supports the required forms and access.
Whether reports identify individual workers or feed performance decisions.
Who can approve stock replenishment.
research_questions: Does direct capture interrupt demonstrations less than the current tally method?
Which validation rules catch real errors without creating unnecessary reviews?
new_work: Review inconsistent counts and explain stock adjustments.
Maintain campaign identifiers, counting definitions, and notification recipients.
Resolve offline synchronisation failures.
tasks.statement: Record and report demonstration-related information, such as the number of questions asked by the audience or the number of coupons distributed.

tasks.short: Sell promoted products, complete checkout and record sales.

steps.what: Discuss suitability, answer objections and agree the customer's purchase choice.
Complete checkout through the point-of-sale system in {OTHER}, with customer payment confirmation.
Copy transaction details into the campaign sales tally.
Export session totals from the point-of-sale system in {OTHER}.
Compare session totals with the tally and flag discrepancies for finance.

tasks.design: Configure approved prices, discounts and campaign codes in the point-of-sale system in {OTHER}. A deterministic connector feeds transaction records to {ERP} and a {BI} campaign view, eliminating the duplicate tally and flagging missing identifiers or inconsistent totals.
tasks.previous_blocker: Campaign reporting often sits outside checkout, so promoters re-enter sales. Payment and finance interfaces require more care than a standalone tally.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing checkout rules and transaction exports support reliable integration. AI-assisted coding can reduce connector development effort without changing payment controls.
tasks.still_hard: Returns, cash differences, offline transactions and attribution across campaigns need agreed treatment. Persuasion and payment confirmation remain human interactions.
tasks.human_edge: Help the customer make a suitable choice and handle objections without inventing claims or discounts.

ambition.what: End-of-session replenishment requests based on promoted-product sales.

tasks.altitude: The promoter spends less time copying and checking totals. With delegated stock-request limits, they can request replenishment after each session; pricing and refund authority do not expand.

reach.task: Investigate incomplete or duplicated sales records.
reach.learn: Use transaction identifiers, return statuses and payment references to trace exceptions.

evidence.claim: Existing checkout configuration can enforce approved prices and discounts while retaining customer payment confirmation.
Structured transaction records can feed campaign reporting and arithmetic checks without a model.

assumptions: The typical setting has a point-of-sale system in {OTHER} and a separate campaign tally.
The solution checks transaction completeness and totals; it does not establish bank settlement.
The connector does not receive payment credentials or initiate charges.
Sales conversation remains the largest time component, consistent with the supplied priors.
unknowns: Whether promoters operate checkout or hand customers to a cashier.
Whether the point-of-sale system in {OTHER} exposes exports, stable identifiers and campaign fields.
How cash, returns and offline transactions are handled.
Whether individual sales reporting triggers consultation under national rules.
Whether replenishment request authority can be delegated.
research_questions: Can a single transaction record satisfy both finance and campaign reporting?
Which exception checks catch real omissions without producing excessive alerts?
new_work: Maintain campaign codes and approved discount configuration.
Review missing transactions, duplicates and returns.
Monitor connector failures and reconcile delayed exports.
Maintain access, retention and GDPR controls for any personal data.
tasks.statement: Sell products being promoted and keep records of sales.

tasks.short: Prepare and arrange a safe, attractive demonstration area.

steps.what: Read the display brief, layout guidance, and equipment checklist.
Inspect the space, customer flow, power supply, and local restrictions.
Collect and move merchandise, signage, equipment, and consumables into position.
Arrange products and signs, connect equipment, and adjust the layout.
Check visibility, accessibility, stability, and safe operation before opening.

tasks.design: Configure approved display templates in the {DOCS} and a preparation form in the {WORKFLOW} to produce a location-specific plan and packing checklist. The demonstrator reviews the plan, inspects the venue, builds the display, and approves readiness on site.
tasks.previous_blocker: Venues and available equipment vary. Most effort involves moving and arranging physical objects.
tasks.enabler_now: Template selection and checklist generation are easy to configure. AI-assisted coding can cheaply add rules for known venue and equipment combinations.
tasks.still_hard: Physical setup, electrical checks, accessibility, and responses to unexpected site conditions stay human. Software cannot validate the actual installation from a planned layout.
tasks.human_edge: The demonstrator sees the real space, adapts the display to customer movement, and checks practical safety.
tasks.altitude: Preparation becomes slightly shorter and missing-kit problems may fall. Most of the week and decision rights remain unchanged.

reach.task: Coordinate demonstration placement with customer flow and store operations.
reach.learn: Merchandising principles, accessibility, site constraints, and local setup authority.

evidence.claim: Templates and deterministic selection rules can generate display plans and packing checklists.
Ordinary software assistance leaves physical assembly and on-site safety judgement with people.

assumptions: Step shares and remaining time are planning estimates, not measured results.
Approved display templates and equipment lists already exist or can be supplied.
The demonstrator is trained and authorised to approve routine setup readiness.
Specialist installation requirements remain outside routine display setup.
The proposed form contains no employee scoring or customer personal data.
Access estimates include checking whether national rules require consultation for the changed work process.
unknowns: Display types, equipment, and venue-specific restrictions.
Who authorises opening and any specialist safety checks.
Availability and accuracy of venue dimensions and equipment lists.
How often missing equipment causes rework.
Whether an existing {WORKFLOW} can generate the checklist.
research_questions: Which venue differences can approved templates represent reliably?
Does a generated packing checklist reduce missing-kit incidents?
new_work: Maintain display templates and equipment lists.
Record venue exceptions for future preparation.
Review generated plans before physical setup.
tasks.statement: Set up and arrange displays or demonstration areas to attract the attention of prospective customers.

tasks.short: Understand customer needs and recommend a suitable product.

steps.what: Ask about intended use, preferences, budget, and relevant constraints.
Consult product information to identify suitable options.
Choose a recommendation and assess unresolved suitability concerns.
Explain the recommendation, discuss trade-offs, and check the customer's response.

tasks.design: Build a small product selector in the {WORKFLOW}, using approved facts from the {DOCS} and explicit compatibility rules. It returns eligible options and a comparison card for the demonstrator to review before recommending a product in conversation.
tasks.previous_blocker: Product facts are spread across leaflets and manuals. Customer preferences do not always fit fixed selection rules.
tasks.enabler_now: Structured product facts and ordinary filters can reduce lookup time. AI-assisted coding makes a focused selector cheaper to build and revise.
tasks.still_hard: Unspoken needs, unusual use cases, and safety-sensitive suitability require judgement. Product information must stay current.
tasks.human_edge: The demonstrator builds trust, notices hesitation, and can advise against a purchase when suitability is doubtful.
tasks.altitude: More time goes into listening and explaining trade-offs, with less searching through product sheets. Decision rights remain unchanged.

reach.task: Check compatibility for an unusual customer use case.
reach.learn: Technical constraints, evidence for claims, and when specialist escalation is necessary.

evidence.claim: Tacton CPQ supports rule-based product configuration; this supports constraint filtering, not conversational suitability judgement.
A shortlist can use explicit product constraints while the person handles preferences and advice.

assumptions: Step shares and remaining time are planning estimates, not measured results.
The demonstration involves ordinary merchandise rather than regulated professional advice.
A basic catalog with stable attributes can support useful filters.
The selector can work with temporary needs data without storing customer identities.
GDPR applies if identifiable customer needs are retained.
The target has no customer-facing AI interaction or employee scoring.
unknowns: Product categories, safety constraints, and applicable sector rules.
Availability and ownership of approved product facts.
Whether compatibility and stock data can be accessed reliably.
How much lookup actually occurs during customer conversations.
Whether any customer needs must be saved in the {CRM}.
research_questions: Which constraints are reliable enough to exclude products automatically?
Do comparison cards improve understanding without distracting from the conversation?
new_work: Review shortlisted options before using them.
Maintain product attributes and compatibility rules.
Escalate needs that the selector cannot represent.
Remove outdated product claims.
tasks.statement: Suggest specific product purchases to meet customers' needs.

tasks.short: Move demonstration materials, assemble them safely, and dismantle and return them after use.

steps.what: Prepare a kit list from the planned demonstration and venue requirements.
Locate, inspect, and pack the listed materials.
Load, transport, and unload the kit at the venue.
Assemble the display, connect equipment, and position materials.
Check stability, connections, access, and safe operation before use.
Disconnect, dismantle, repack, and return the materials after the session.
Update the shared kit register with returns, missing items, and damage.

tasks.design: A deterministic generator on the {DATA_PLATFORM} combines venue requirements and kit rules from the {DOCS} into a packing list. Configure a kit register and exception form in the {WORKFLOW}, linking each kit to current assembly instructions and routing repair requests while people move, assemble, and inspect it.
tasks.previous_blocker: Most effort is physical. Administrative automation needs a reliable kit catalogue, and local layouts do not follow one universal plan.
tasks.enabler_now: Simple rule tables and mobile forms can handle lists and records. AI-assisted coding reduces the effort of building a small generator; it does not automate handling materials.
tasks.still_hard: Loading, lifting, site access, damaged equipment, and physical safety checks remain. Incorrect inventory data can still produce an unusable kit list.
tasks.human_edge: Notice damage or instability, adapt the layout, and stop use when equipment is unsafe.
tasks.altitude: The week remains dominated by moving and setting up materials, with less list preparation and return paperwork. Decision rights do not change.

reach.task: Plan floor space and access for an in-store demonstration.
reach.learn: Local display restrictions, customer circulation, and practical setup constraints.

evidence.claim: Rule-based packing lists and shared registers can reduce administration without automating physical setup.

assumptions: The promoter handles a portable kit rather than a specialist installation.
A shared {SPREADSHEET} register is a plausible current means, not a confirmed customer fact.
The supplied coordination prior includes physical handling; it does not imply software can perform it.
The target uses a simple configured register before considering an operations integration.
unknowns: Actual kit sizes, lifting needs, transport arrangements, and safety responsibilities.
Whether a kit register already exists in the {OPS_SYSTEM} or {WORKFLOW}.
Who maintains assembly instructions and authorises repairs.
Access to the kit catalogue and approved venue requirements.
Whether national rules require consultation for changed working practices.
research_questions: Which kit combinations can be represented with fixed selection rules?
Can standard packing layouts reduce handling time through equipment redesign?
new_work: Maintain the kit catalogue and compatibility rules.
Record damage and reconcile missing items.
Check generated lists when venue requirements change.
Keep assembly and safety instructions current.
tasks.statement: Transport, assemble, and disassemble materials used in presentations.

tasks.short: Identify interested customers, assess their needs, and give relevant information or arrange follow-up.

steps.what: Notice visitors who show interest in the demonstration.
Ask about intended use, constraints, timing, and interest.
Decide whether the customer needs information, a sales referral, or no follow-up.
Find approved information matching the customer's needs.
Explain suitable options and agree whether the customer wants follow-up.
Enter contact details, needs, and agreed follow-up into the {CRM}.

tasks.design: Configure a short mobile form in the {CRM} with qualification prompts, duplicate checks, and internal routing. Tag approved answers in the {DOCS} by use and constraint, so the promoter can select relevant information while keeping qualification and customer conversations human.
tasks.previous_blocker: Interest emerges during live conversation. Existing forms often take too long at a busy stand, and approved information is scattered.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing form and search configuration can remove much of the paperwork. AI-assisted coding can make a small connector cheaper when native links are missing.
tasks.still_hard: Distinguishing curiosity from buying intent needs tact. Missing customer information and crowded venues limit reliable capture.
tasks.human_edge: Read hesitation, ask respectful questions, and recognise when further selling would be unwelcome.

ambition.what: An agreed handover to a sales representative with the customer's use case already captured

tasks.altitude: The promoter spends less time finding information and entering records. They can choose the referral route within agreed criteria; pricing and commercial approval rights do not change.

reach.task: Prepare the first discovery call from the lead record.
reach.learn: Which use-case details make a referral useful and which commitments require sales approval.

evidence.claim: Live qualification remains conversational; structured capture and routing can use existing records software.
GDPR requires a lawful basis, limited collection, and appropriate retention for identifiable prospect records.

assumptions: Qualification means product fit and readiness for follow-up, not credit assessment.
Most time is spent face to face, consistent with the supplied priors.
The {CRM} supports mobile entry, configurable fields, and internal assignment.
Time shares and remaining percentages are planning estimates.
unknowns: The customer's qualification criteria and permitted referral decisions.
Available {CRM} permissions and mobile connectivity.
The lawful basis, follow-up permissions, and retention policy.
Whether national rules require employee consultation for changed working practices.
research_questions: Which captured fields predict a useful handover without lengthening the conversation?
Can existing configuration provide routing and duplicate checks without custom integration?
new_work: Maintain qualification prompts and approved-answer tags.
Resolve duplicate records and failed assignments.
Check that contact preferences match the agreed follow-up.
Review referral usefulness with sales representatives.
tasks.statement: Identify interested and qualified customers to provide them with additional information.

tasks.short: Rehearse demonstrations, collect feedback, and correct problems before presenting to customers.

steps.what: Review the current script, product facts, and demonstration instructions.
Run the demonstration aloud with the actual materials and equipment.
Give feedback on clarity, pacing, handling, and likely customer questions.
Revise the script and practice cues using the feedback.

loop.input: Current demo script, free-text rehearsal notes, approved product brief, and fixed safety instructions.
loop.output: A revised script with changed passages and references to approved facts.
loop.check: Reject changes to fixed safety instructions. Require product-claim references, then have the sales supervisor check meaning and approve use.
loop.stop: One draft and at most one correction pass per revision. Missing support or unresolved contradictions return to manual editing.
loop.why_not_simpler: Templates handle structure but cannot reliably rewrite varied coaching notes into clear spoken passages. Use manual editing if scripts rarely change.

steps.what: Repeat the changed sections and decide whether the demonstration is ready.

tasks.design: Configure versioned rehearsal packs in the {DOCS}, combining the approved script, product facts, and fixed safety instructions. A bounded drafting loop on the {DATA_PLATFORM} proposes script changes from rehearsal notes; the sales supervisor approves changes before use, while rehearsal and readiness decisions stay human.
tasks.previous_blocker: Useful feedback is contextual, and physical fluency develops through practice. Rewriting notes into a script takes time, but unchecked generated claims would be unreliable.
tasks.enabler_now: Versioned documents and small drafting loops can support controlled revisions. Source references and fixed safety sections make review more concrete; they do not guarantee correctness.
tasks.still_hard: A fluent script does not prove confident delivery or safe handling. Coaching quality, product changes, and approval delays still affect readiness.
tasks.human_edge: Develop physical fluency, notice confusing explanations, and give supportive feedback that improves confidence.

ambition.what: A venue-specific rehearsal pack for demonstrations with unfamiliar audience questions

tasks.altitude: Less preparation and editing time leaves more room for focused rehearsal. The promoter can propose tailored wording; approval of product claims and safety instructions stays with the existing responsible roles.

reach.task: Coach a demonstration for a new audience.
reach.learn: How to turn specific feedback into practice goals and distinguish wording problems from skill gaps.

evidence.claim: A bounded model can draft script revisions from notes, but factual accuracy and delivery still need human review.
EU AI Act Article 4 requires measures to ensure sufficient AI literacy for staff using the drafting system.

assumptions: Rehearsal includes periodic supervisor feedback, rather than supervision of every practice session.
No recording, automated employee scoring, or performance-ranking system is introduced.
Safety instructions remain fixed and version controlled.
The revision loop is worthwhile only when tailoring scripts is recurring work.
Build ranges cover a narrow pilot; formal consultation timelines may exceed them.
unknowns: How often scripts change and who approves them.
Whether approved product facts are complete and current.
Whether rehearsal notes are retained as employee records and for how long.
Permitted model processing, document access, and data location.
Applicable national rules and required employee or works-council consultation.
research_questions: Does a reviewed draft save time compared with editing an existing template?
Which rehearsal problems require physical practice rather than script changes?
Can unsupported claims and altered safety instructions be reliably caught during validation?
new_work: Review proposed script changes and source references.
Maintain approved facts, fixed instructions, and drafting prompts.
Handle unsupported claims and contradictory coaching notes.
Train reviewers to assess generated text.
Manage rehearsal-note access and retention.
tasks.statement: Practice demonstrations to ensure that they will run smoothly.

tasks.short: Adapt demonstration presentations to the audience while preserving accurate product claims.

steps.what: Clarify audience knowledge, interests, language and available demonstration time.
Find approved slides, product claims, images and demonstration instructions.
Adapt examples, sequence and speaker notes, then assemble presentation materials.

loop.input: Audience brief, approved content blocks, claim references and presentation constraints.
loop.output: Selected content order, adapted examples and speaker notes in a fixed template.
loop.check: Preserve protected claims and warnings; require source references and validate template structure and length.
loop.stop: One draft and one repair pass; unsupported requests return as gaps for the demonstrator.
loop.why_not_simpler: Templates handle layout, but audience-specific examples and explanations require language adaptation.

steps.what: Rehearse the presentation and judge clarity, timing and audience fit.
Check final claims, apply revisions and release the presentation for use.

tasks.design: Configure an approved content library in the {DOCS}, then combine deterministic template assembly with a bounded loop for examples and speaker notes. The {WORKFLOW} routes the finished presentation for approval after rehearsal, preserving source references and protected warnings.
tasks.previous_blocker: Reusable content exists, but selecting, rewriting and assembling it for each audience takes manual effort.
tasks.enabler_now: Document assembly is established; bounded language drafting and AI-assisted coding make a small adaptation tool cheaper to build.
tasks.still_hard: Audience fit is uncertain until delivery, and a fluent rewrite can alter a technical claim or omit a warning.
tasks.human_edge: Choose examples that resonate, judge physical feasibility and adjust explanations to the audience's reactions.

ambition.what: Beginner audiences receiving a plain-language demonstration variant.

tasks.altitude: The week shifts from copying and editing materials toward rehearsal and audience discovery. The demonstrator can select approved presentation variants; new technical claims still require product-specialist approval.

reach.role: sales representative of technical and scientific products
reach.task: Prepare audience-specific sales explanations from approved technical material.
reach.learn: Audience discovery, evidence-backed benefits and clear technical storytelling.

evidence.claim: Template assembly with bounded language adaptation is technically feasible; no direct demonstrator presentation case appears in the digest.
EU AI Act Article 4 addresses AI literacy, relevant to staff using the drafting tool.
Time shares and build ranges are estimates; this preparation task has more document work than its means prior suggests.

assumptions: A pilot covers one product family, one presentation template and approved source material.
Audience briefs describe group needs without individual profiling.
The demonstrator may approve adaptations that preserve existing claims; new claims go to a product specialist.
GDPR applies to any personal data introduced into audience briefs; access and retention must follow the existing lawful purpose.
Access planning includes an employee consultation check under national rules where applicable.
unknowns: Are approved content blocks labelled by product version, language and audience?
Which changes require product-specialist approval?
Which presentation formats and accessibility standards are required?
research_questions: How reliably do checks catch altered claims and omitted warnings?
Do beginner audiences understand the adapted variant better during teach-back?
Does rehearsal time remain stable when assembly time falls?
new_work: Review final claims, examples and warnings before release.
Maintain templates, protected content blocks and source references.
Sample drafts for factual drift and improve validation rules.
Train demonstrators to recognise unsupported generated content.
tasks.statement: Prepare or alter presentation contents to target specific audiences.

tasks.short: Learn competitor facts and customer concerns to give more useful answers.

steps.what: Ask customers about interests, doubts and previous product experiences.
Exchange recurring questions and competitor observations with teammates.
Find relevant product specifications, competitor materials and approved answers.
Turn source material into comparison notes and possible answers.

loop.input: Selected source passages and anonymous customer concerns.
loop.output: A short answer brief with source references and explicit gaps.
loop.check: Require a source passage for each factual claim; flag conflicting dates and specifications.
loop.stop: One draft and one validation pass per brief; unresolved claims go to a product specialist.
loop.why_not_simpler: Free-text concerns and differently worded source materials need interpretation.

steps.what: Check proposed answers and select what can be used with customers.

tasks.design: Configure indexed product and competitor materials in the {DOCS}, with links to public material in the {CMS}. A bounded drafting loop creates a sourced answer brief; the demonstrator checks it before customer use and routes unsupported claims through the {WORKFLOW}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Source material is scattered, and customer concerns rarely match the wording of product documents.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing search and inexpensive document processing can support a small, source-bound drafting service.
tasks.still_hard: Competitor facts become stale, comparisons may be misleading, and customers often reveal concerns indirectly.
tasks.human_edge: Ask useful follow-up questions and recognise when the stated objection hides a different concern.

ambition.what: Weekly selection of one unanswered customer concern for a targeted demonstration.

tasks.altitude: The week contains less searching and note assembly. The demonstrator gains scope to choose learning priorities within approved messaging; authority to approve new product claims stays with the product specialist.

reach.task: Build evidence-based answers to technical objections.
reach.learn: Specification interpretation, fair comparison and clear escalation of unsupported claims.

evidence.claim: Indexed source retrieval and source-bound brief drafting are plausible building blocks; no direct demonstrator case appears in the digest.
Time shares, remaining effort and build ranges are planning estimates, not measured results.

assumptions: A pilot covers one product family and a small approved competitor set.
Search uses labelled documents and product fields before adding semantic interpretation.
Customer concerns are recorded anonymously; conversations are not recorded.
Source checking takes more time than the means prior suggests because this task specifically concerns learning.
unknowns: Which product and competitor materials are available with reuse rights?
Who approves comparative claims and maintains source versions?
Can demonstrators access the source library during events?
research_questions: Can reviewers trace every proposed comparison to a current source?
Does the brief improve answer accuracy on unfamiliar customer questions?
new_work: Review answer briefs and resolve unsupported comparisons.
Retire expired source material and maintain product labels.
Check that concern notes contain no unnecessary personal data.
tasks.statement: Learn about competitors' products or consumers' interests or concerns to answer questions or provide more complete information.

tasks.short: Coordinate with fellow demonstrators to serve large crowds safely and effectively.

steps.what: Check the event roster, demonstration schedule and venue constraints.
Agree team positions, hand signals, rotations and escalation arrangements.
Welcome visitors and direct them to available demonstrations.

tasks.short: Turn customer reactions and demonstration experience into product or service improvement recommendations.
